title: Conservation of biodiversity
introduction: What is being lost during the biodiversity crisis, how can scientists measure it, and which interventions can prevent irreversible loss?
objectives: Differentiate genetic, species and ecosystem diversity
Analyse case studies and distinguish global extinction from local loss
Interpret real population indices and explicitly modelled survey counts
Justify combined conservation approaches and EDGE prioritization

sections.guidingQuestion: What is lost when biodiversity declines?
sections.explanation:
Biodiversity includes genetic diversity within populations, differences among species, and the variety of ecosystems and ecological interactions. Genetic diversity represents heritable variants available within a species. Species diversity combines the number of species with how evenly individuals are distributed among them, while ecosystem diversity reflects varied habitats, communities and processes.

These levels interact. Habitat fragmentation can reduce gene flow between populations even before any species disappears; loss of one specialist species can also alter ecosystem functioning. A study must say whether it measures alleles, species richness, relative abundance or habitats instead of referring to a single unmeasured 'biodiversity score'.

A forest may still contain the same number of tree species after selective removal, yet lose genetic variants within a rare tree species and have reduced evenness. Species count alone would miss these changes.

A study reporting a diversity 'increase' should name the scale: newly detected alleles, changes in species relative abundances, or recovery of distinct habitats. A conservation project can improve one component while another deteriorates, so an overall conclusion requires multiple measurements.
sections.revisionSummary: Genetic, species and ecosystem diversity; richness is species count, evenness describes relative abundance.
terms: Species richness: number of species recorded
Species evenness: relative balance of individuals among species

sections.guidingQuestion: Why can scientists not count every species alive now or in the past?
sections.explanation:
Scientists have described millions of living species, while many remain undescribed, particularly among microorganisms and invertebrates. Historical diversity is reconstructed indirectly from fossils, which provide strong evidence of evolutionary change but preserve only a small and uneven subset of past organisms and environments.

The Guide notes an inference that more species may be alive today than at earlier times. This is not a directly counted historical total: preservation, sampling and differences in taxonomic species concepts affect comparisons. Extinction and speciation have repeatedly changed species richness over geological time, while present species estimates have substantial uncertainty.

Soft-bodied forest organisms are underrepresented in fossils compared with animals bearing mineralized shells. A fossil-rich marine interval cannot be naively compared with an equally long terrestrial interval without correcting sampling differences.

Fossils strongly demonstrate that species existed and disappeared in geological time, but fossil formation and discovery are highly selective. Whether present diversity exceeds every past interval is an inference with uncertainty; a claimed numerical total requires stated classification and sampling assumptions.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can distinct human pressures eliminate local populations or entire species?
sections.explanation:
North Island giant moa (Dinornis novaezealandiae) disappeared after human settlement of New Zealand. Moa extinction is strongly linked to human hunting and habitat change. Caribbean monk seals (Neomonachus tropicalis, historically Monachus tropicalis) were hunted intensively for products such as oil and have been recognized as globally extinct following historical decline and long absence of confirmed records.

A geographically relevant contrast is the Syrian brown bear (Ursus arctos syriacus): Lebanese biodiversity reports identify it as extirpated from Lebanon, while brown bears persist elsewhere in their range. This is local extinction, not global species extinction. A defensible case study separates direct evidence from inferred drivers; the exact proportion of hunting versus other pressures need not be invented. The three cases show terrestrial megafaunal extinction, marine species extinction and local mammal disappearance.

A conservation student sorting the three records should label moa and Caribbean monk seal global losses but Lebanese Syrian brown bear an extirpation from one country. Reintroducing bears would address local recovery, not reverse global extinction.

North Island giant moa and Caribbean monk seal are globally extinct, while the Syrian brown bear case documents local disappearance from Lebanon. Historical sightings, records of exploitation and habitat conversion support causal interpretations to different degrees. Do not convert local absence into evidence of global extinction.
sections.revisionSummary: North Island giant moa: global; Caribbean monk seal: global; Syrian brown bear in Lebanon: local extirpation.
terms: Global extinction: no living members of a species survive
Extirpation: disappearance from a specified geographic area
sections.workedExample: A conservation student sorting the three records should label moa and Caribbean monk seal global losses but Lebanese Syrian brown bear an extirpation from one country. Reintroducing bears would address local recovery, not reverse global extinction.

misconceptions.misconception: The Syrian brown bear has disappeared everywhere because it disappeared from Lebanon.
misconceptions.correction: Extirpation means local disappearance; populations of a species may remain elsewhere.

sections.guidingQuestion: What ecological differences arise when natural ecosystems are cleared or fragmented?
sections.explanation:
Mixed dipterocarp forests of Southeast Asia have multi-layered canopies, diverse tree species, epiphytes, forest-floor organisms and specialized microclimates. Logging changes structure, while full conversion to oil-palm monoculture removes much of the original community and its specialized niches. Research in Borneo shows that even repeatedly logged forest can retain many original bird and dung-beetle species and has substantially more conservation value than land converted entirely to plantations.

A contrasting coastal example is the loss and fragmentation of Lebanese Mediterranean dune habitats, including reported dune disappearance along the Akkar coast associated with sand extraction and other land-use pressures. Dunes are ecological systems, not simply empty beaches: vegetation stabilizes substrate and supports associated fauna. This case must be evaluated using geographically located surveys and historical imagery rather than invented measurements. Natural disturbances can affect ecosystems too, but the required focus here is anthropogenic loss.

Compare a selectively logged forest, which still retains trees and many dependent species, with a fully cleared oil-palm plantation. In a local dune investigation, compare dated aerial images of the same coastal stretch and record remaining vegetated dunes.

Mixed dipterocarp forest conversion to monoculture eliminates many canopy niches and ecological relationships. However, selectively logged forest may still support substantial biodiversity and should not be dismissed as ecologically empty. For Lebanese dunes, matched satellite dates, locations and ground truthing are required before quantifying reported habitat loss.
sections.revisionSummary: Southeast Asian mixed dipterocarp forest conversion to plantations; Lebanon/Akkar coastal dune loss through sand extraction and land use.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can repeat surveys distinguish changes in richness, evenness and abundance?
sections.explanation:
Biodiversity assessment requires consistent repeated surveys of many habitats with documented sampling effort. Species richness counts detected species, while evenness compares their relative abundances. A decline in average population size can occur without local extinction, and a richness count can remain constant while the community becomes dominated by one species.

WWF's 2024 Living Planet Index reported an average 73% decline in the relative sizes of the monitored vertebrate populations from 1970 to 2020. That statistic is an index of monitored population trends: it does not mean 73% of species or individual animals vanished. The classroom table below uses invented, explicitly hypothetical counts to illustrate why evenness matters; these numbers must not be presented as research observations. Real findings demand published methods, suitable controls, repeat sampling and critical assessment of citizen-science detection bias.

In a constructed survey, site X has 10, 10 and 10 individuals of three species in year 1, then 28, 1 and 1 in year 2. Richness remains three and totals remain 30, but relative abundance becomes much less even.

Compare richness and evenness using equal-area plots, consistent methods and comparable effort over repeated dates. The WWF 2024 Living Planet Index describes the average proportional change among monitored vertebrate population trends; the reported decline is neither a species-extinction fraction nor a census of every animal.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can human population pressure affect multiple extinction pathways?
sections.explanation:
Growth in human population and consumption can increase demand for land, food, timber, fish and materials, though impacts also depend strongly on production methods and resource inequality. Direct drivers include excessive hunting and fishing, urbanization, deforestation, land conversion for agriculture, chemical and nutrient pollution, and species or disease spread through global transport.

Drivers reinforce one another. Fragmented populations have fewer opportunities for dispersal and genetic exchange; invasive organisms can then disrupt ecological relationships, while climate change compounds existing stresses. Conservation assessments should distinguish an immediate driver (for example clearing habitat) from broader societal causes and should avoid treating all people or regions as having identical environmental footprints.

A wetland drained for housing loses vegetation and water-storage functions; pollutant runoff and introduced predators can further reduce survival of the remaining species.

Habitat clearance reduces the area available to specialist organisms; fragmentation can interrupt dispersal; trade can introduce invasive species and pathogens; overexploitation removes organisms faster than reproduction replaces them. Human population growth can intensify these pressures but impacts depend on consumption, land use and management, not head count alone.
sections.revisionSummary: Overexploitation, urbanization, agricultural clearance, pollution and invasive species/disease spread (any four).

sections.guidingQuestion: Why is one conservation strategy rarely sufficient?
sections.explanation:
In situ conservation protects organisms within the habitats and communities where they naturally live; reserves require management, monitoring and enforcement. Rewilding and ecological restoration can re-establish processes or repair degraded habitats. Ex situ work maintains threatened organisms or their germplasm away from the original wild population, including zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks and tissue collections.

Methods have distinct strengths and limits. A seed bank can preserve genetic material but does not protect a forest's soil, fungi or pollination network. A reserve may retain ecological interactions but fail if it is poorly connected or inadequately managed. Captive breeding may support reintroduction only where habitat and threats are addressed and genetic and welfare risks are managed.

For a threatened native tree, protect surviving forest stands, collect genetically diverse seeds under appropriate storage protocols, restore suitable sites and monitor recruitment over years. Seed storage alone cannot regenerate the full forest community.

In situ protected areas conserve ecological interactions, while rewilding or ecological restoration aims to recover damaged ecosystem processes. sections.guidingQuestion: What does the EDGE of Existence conservation approach measure?
sections.explanation:
The EDGE programme prioritizes species that combine high evolutionary distinctiveness—representing long or relatively unshared branches of the Tree of Life—with high global endangerment, a measure of extinction threat. The rationale is that preventing the loss of a deeply distinct threatened lineage safeguards evolutionary history that cannot simply be replaced by saving a close relative.

EDGE values depend on the phylogeny and IUCN risk assessments used, both subject to revision and uncertainty. Prioritization is not the same as assigning intrinsic moral worth; it must also consider ecological roles, cost, local communities, feasibility and equity. A common species with many close relatives may score lower for distinctiveness without being ecologically unimportant.

If two threatened species face similar extinction risk but one belongs to a long isolated evolutionary branch, EDGE may prioritize that branch. The conclusion can differ when threats, feasibility or local ecological roles are incorporated.

EDGE considers evolutionary distinctiveness from phylogenetic branches together with global extinction risk, using evidence such as the IUCN Red List. Scores can change with a revised tree or threat category; selecting projects must still consider feasibility, local community priorities and ecological roles.

questions.prompt: What is lost when biodiversity declines?

options.text: It spans genetic, species and ecosystem diversity.
options.feedback: Genetic, species and ecosystem diversity; richness is species count, evenness describes relative abundance.

options.text: It counts only rare mammals.
options.feedback: Genetic, species and ecosystem-level diversity all matter; richness alone omits relative abundance.

options.text: It ignores variation among individuals of one species.

options.text: It is identical to the number of trees.

questions.prompt: A restored wetland records more plant species but fewer genetic variants in its rare reed population. Explain why one overall biodiversity verdict is insufficient.
questions.answer: Species diversity can increase while genetic diversity within a focal species decreases. The assessment must separately report species and within-species genetic measures.
markingPoints: Species diversity can increase while genetic diversity within a focal species decreases.
The assessment must separately report species and within-species genetic measures.

questions.prompt: Why can scientists not count every species alive now or in the past?

options.text: Today's named species are a partial count and fossil records sample the past unevenly.
options.feedback: Undiscovered living species; incomplete and biased fossil preservation/sampling.

options.text: Every living species has been described.
options.feedback: Fossil preservation is selective and many species, past and present, remain unrecorded.

options.text: Soft-bodied animals always fossilize better than shells.
options.feedback: Fossil preservation is selective and many species, past and present, remain unrecorded.

options.text: Fossil absence is definitive proof a species did not exist.
options.feedback: Fossil preservation is selective and many species, past and present, remain unrecorded.

questions.prompt: Two fossil intervals yield different species counts. Give one reason this cannot by itself establish that biological diversity was lower in the smaller sample.
questions.answer: Rock exposure, preservation conditions or sampling intensity may differ between intervals. Taxonomic criteria and the incompleteness of the fossil record limit direct comparisons.

Taxonomic criteria and the incompleteness of the fossil record limit direct comparisons.

questions.answer: It summarizes relative changes in sizes of monitored vertebrate populations from 1970–2020. It does not imply that 73% of species became extinct or 73% of individual animals were counted as lost.
markingPoints: It summarizes relative changes in sizes of monitored vertebrate populations from 1970–2020.
It does not imply that 73% of species became extinct or 73% of individual animals were counted as lost.

questions.prompt: Using the constructed counts, explain how richness and evenness change between the two periods. Treat all counts as hypothetical, not field data.
questions.answer: Richness remains three species, and total count remains 30, but evenness decreases because A rises to 28/30 and the other two species each fall to 1/30.
markingPoints: Both periods contain three species, so richness is unchanged.
The second distribution is more dominated by A, so evenness declines.

summary: Biodiversity includes genetic, species and ecosystem variety. Distinct human pressures drive local and global losses; repeated evidence and complementary, ethically considered approaches are necessary to conserve threatened evolutionary history.
